metadata.file_name: 174. Courtney et al. (2022). The influence of ICT use and related attitudes on students’ math and science performance: multilevel analyses of the last decade’s PISA surveys.pdf
metadata.title: The influence of ICT use and related attitudes on students’ math and science performance: multilevel analyses of the last decade’s PISA surveys

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study merges student and school data from PISA 2009, 2012, 2015, and 2018 for countries that administered the ICT questionnaire modules. Analytic samples exclude schools with fewer than ten students and account for missing ICT-related data, yielding cycle-specific totals of students and schools. To make countries contribute equally, the authors use “senate weights” and then rescale them within each country so the sum of student senate weights equals 5000 per country (constant computed using the number of students in the final analyses after missing-data accounting). The manuscript reports using normalized weights in all multilevel models; replicate-weight methodology (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is not described, and the analysis is implemented in R using lme4 maximum-likelihood estimation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used merged PISA 2009, 2012, 2015, and 2018 student and school datasets for countries that opted into the ICT survey modules. For each cycle, schools with fewer than ten students were removed. The authors also account for missing ICT-related data (and other variables used in the models), and the senate weights are rescaled using the number of students included in the final analyses after accounting for missing data. Analyses are run separately by year and subject (math/science) using all available plausible values for that cycle.

confounders_identified.variable_name: ICT as topic in social interaction
ICT use at school in general
Perceived autonomy related to ICT use

top_predictors: Perceived autonomy related to ICT use (AUTICT)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Three-level linear mixed-effects models (maximum likelihood) using all available plausible values per cycle; reported as mean unstandardized coefficients (b) with t values and p values. Substantive effects threshold: p<0.001 and b>2 scale-score points at student/school levels; country-level interest p<0.05.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009/2012/2015/2018 the study leveraged student ESCS, gender, and ICT-related attitudes (especially perceived autonomy related to ICT use, plus ICT interest and perceived ICT competence) to model mathematics achievement (Plausible Values), finding that ICT availability and ICT use inside/outside school were generally neutral or negatively associated with math performance, while positive ICT attitudes and beliefs showed substantive positive associations across cycles. This indicates that policies should prioritize strengthening students’ ICT-related motivation, competence beliefs, and autonomy (quality and purposeful use) rather than increasing raw ICT access or frequency of use, while recognizing the study is cross-sectional and estimates associations rather than causal effects.

top_predictors: Perceived autonomy related to ICT use (AUTICT)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Three-level linear mixed-effects models (maximum likelihood) using all available plausible values per cycle; reported as mean unstandardized coefficients (b) with t values and p values. Substantive effects threshold: p<0.001 and b>2 scale-score points at student/school levels; country-level interest p<0.05.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009/2012/2015/2018 the study leveraged student ESCS, gender, and ICT-related attitudes (especially perceived autonomy related to ICT use, plus ICT interest and perceived ICT competence) to model science achievement (Plausible Values), finding that ICT availability and ICT use inside/outside school were mostly neutral or negatively associated with science performance, whereas positive ICT attitudes and beliefs were substantively and consistently positively associated with science achievement across cycles. This indicates that educational practice should focus on cultivating students’ self-confidence, competence beliefs, and autonomy in ICT use as part of learning design, rather than assuming that greater ICT access or more frequent ICT use will automatically improve science outcomes.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes four PISA cycles (2009, 2012, 2015, 2018) using merged student and school data to examine how ICT availability, ICT use (inside and outside school), and ICT-related attitudes relate to mathematics and science achievement. Achievement is modeled using PISA plausible values, and the authors fit three-level linear mixed-effects models with students nested in schools and schools nested in countries, using maximum likelihood estimation. They report that ICT availability and ICT use are generally neutral or negatively associated with math and science performance, while ICT attitudes and beliefs—particularly perceived autonomy related to ICT use—show the strongest positive associations (e.g., autonomy coefficients around b≈8.93–9.43 for math and b≈10.20–11.90 for science in 2015/2018). The models explain up to about 9.5% of student-level residual variance, and country-level GDP per capita shows inconsistent associations (significant mainly in 2012). Because PISA is cross-sectional and ICT questionnaire items vary across cycles, the results support associations rather than causal claims.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The paper does not train or evaluate machine-learning predictive models; it uses three-level linear mixed-effects modeling with plausible values. Therefore, ML technique fields are intentionally empty (no ML algorithms to extract), while the study still provides substantive multilevel association results across PISA cycles.
